title: Book 5, Chapter 15 — Tenth Year of the War—Death of Cleon and Brasidas—Peace of Nicias
paragraphs: The next summer the truce for a year came to an end, having lasted until the Pythian games. During the armistice the Athenians drove the Delians out of Delos. They concluded that the Delians must have been polluted by some old offense at the time of their consecration, and that this was what the earlier purification of the island had left undone; as I have related, that purification had been thought complete once the graves of the dead were removed. Pharnaces gave the Delians Atramyttium in Asia, and they settled there when they left Delos.

Meanwhile Cleon persuaded the Athenians to let him sail, when the armistice expired, to the towns in the direction of Thrace. He took twelve hundred heavy infantry and three hundred horse from Athens, a large force of the allies, and thirty ships. He first touched at Scione, which was still under siege, and took some heavy infantry from the army there. Then he sailed into Cophos, a harbor in the territory of Torone, not far from the town. From there he learned from deserters that Brasidas was not in Torone, and that its garrison was too weak to give him battle. He therefore advanced against the town with his army, and sent ten ships to sail around into the harbor. He came first to the fortification that Brasidas had recently thrown up in front of the town to take in the suburb; to do this Brasidas had pulled down part of the original wall and made the whole one city. Pasitelidas, the Lacedaemonian commander, hurried to this point with whatever garrison the place had, to repel the Athenian assault. But he was hard pressed, and when he saw the ships that had been sent around sailing into the harbor, he began to fear that they would reach the city before its defenders were there. He feared too that, with the fortification also carried, he would be taken prisoner, so he abandoned the outwork and ran into the town. But the Athenians from the ships had already taken Torone, and their land forces, following at his heels, burst in with him in a rush over the part of the old wall that had been pulled down. They killed some of the Peloponnesians and Toronaeans in the melee and took the rest prisoner, among them Pasitelidas their commander. Brasidas meanwhile had advanced to relieve Torone, and had only about four miles still to go when he heard on the road that it had fallen, and he turned back. Cleon and the Athenians set up two trophies, one by the harbor and the other by the fortification. They made slaves of the wives and children of the Toronaeans, and sent the men to Athens, together with the Peloponnesians and any Chalcidians who were there, seven hundred in all. All of these came home afterwards, however: the Peloponnesians when peace was concluded, and the rest by exchange for other prisoners held by the Olynthians. About the same time the Boeotians took Panactum, a fortress on the Athenian border, by treachery. Meanwhile Cleon put a garrison in Torone, weighed anchor, and sailed around Athos on his way to Amphipolis.

About the same time Phaeax, son of Erasistratus, set sail from Athens with two colleagues as ambassador to Italy and Sicily. After the Athenians left Sicily following the pacification, the Leontines had enrolled a number of new citizens, and the commons planned to redivide the land. The upper classes saw what they intended, called in the Syracusans, and expelled the commons. The commons were scattered in various directions. The upper classes then came to an agreement with the Syracusans, abandoned and laid waste their city, and went to live at Syracuse, where they were made citizens. Afterwards some of them became dissatisfied, left Syracuse, and occupied Phocaeae, a quarter of the town of Leontini, and Bricinniae, a strong place in the Leontine country. Most of the exiled commons joined them there, and they carried on the war from the fortifications. When the Athenians heard this, they sent Phaeax to see whether they could somehow convince their allies there and the rest of the Sicilians of the ambitious designs of Syracuse, so as to bring them into a general coalition against her and thus save the commons of Leontini. Arriving in Sicily, Phaeax succeeded at Camarina and Agrigentum, but was rebuffed at Gela. He did not go on to the rest, since he saw that he would not succeed with them. He returned through the country of the Sicels to Catana, visited Bricinniae on the way and encouraged its inhabitants, and sailed back to Athens.

On his voyage along the coast to and from Sicily, he negotiated with some cities in Italy about friendship with Athens. He also met some Locrian settlers who had been exiled from Messina. They had been sent there when the Locrians were called in by one of the factions that divided Messina after the pacification of Sicily, and Messina had for a time fallen into the hands of the Locrians. Phaeax met these settlers on their way home and did them no harm, since the Locrians had agreed with him on a treaty with Athens. They were the only people among the allies who, when the Sicilians were reconciled, had not made peace with Athens; nor would they have done so now, had they not been pressed by a war with the Hipponians and Medmaeans, who lived on their border and were colonists of theirs. Phaeax meanwhile continued his voyage and at length arrived at Athens.

Cleon, whom we left sailing from Torone to Amphipolis, made Eion his base. He made an unsuccessful assault on Stagirus, a colony of Andros, and took Galepsus, a colony of Thasos, by storm. He then sent envoys to Perdiccas, commanding him to attend with an army as the alliance required, and others to Thrace, to Polles, king of the Odomantians, who was to bring as many Thracian mercenaries as possible. He himself remained inactive at Eion, waiting for them to arrive. Brasidas, informed of this, took up an observation post of his own on Cerdylium. This place lies in the Argilian country on high ground across the river, not far from Amphipolis, and it commands a view on all sides. It made it impossible for Cleon’s army to move without his seeing it. For he fully expected that Cleon, despising the small numbers of his opponent, would march against Amphipolis with the force he had with him. At the same time Brasidas made his preparations. He called to his standard fifteen hundred Thracian mercenaries and all the Edonians, horse and targeteers. He also had a thousand Myrcinian and Chalcidian targeteers, besides those in Amphipolis, and heavy infantry numbering about two thousand in all, and three hundred Hellenic horse. Fifteen hundred of these he had with him on Cerdylium; the rest were stationed with Clearidas in Amphipolis.

After remaining quiet for some time, Cleon was at length forced to do what Brasidas expected. His soldiers were tired of the inactivity. They also began to reflect seriously on the weakness and incompetence of their commander, on the skill and valor that would be set against him, and on their own original unwillingness to go with him. These murmurs reached Cleon. He resolved not to disgust the army by keeping it in one place, so he broke up his camp and advanced. His temper was what it had been at Pylos, where his success had given him confidence in his own ability. He never dreamed that anyone would come out to fight him. He said he was going up rather to view the place; and if he was waiting for his reinforcements, it was not to make victory certain in case he should be compelled to fight, but to be able to surround and storm the city. He accordingly came and posted his army on a strong hill in front of Amphipolis, and went on to examine the lake formed by the Strymon and how the town lay on the side of Thrace. He thought he could retire whenever he pleased without fighting, since no one was to be seen on the wall or coming out of the gates, all of which were shut. Indeed, it seemed a mistake not to have brought siege engines with him; he could then have taken the town, as there was no one to defend it.

As soon as Brasidas saw the Athenians in motion, he came down from Cerdylium himself and entered Amphipolis. He did not venture to go out in regular order against the Athenians. He mistrusted his strength and thought it inadequate to the attempt: not in numbers, since these were not so unequal, but in quality, for the flower of the Athenian army was in the field, with the best of the Lemnians and Imbrians. He therefore prepared to attack them by stratagem. He thought he would have less chance of beating the enemy if he showed him the number of his troops and the shifts he had been put to in arming them, than if he kept them out of sight and so denied him the knowledge of how good a right he had to despise them. He accordingly picked out a hundred and fifty heavy infantry and put the rest under Clearidas. He determined to attack suddenly, before the Athenians retired; he thought he would not again have such a chance of catching them alone, once their reinforcements were allowed to come up. So he called all his soldiers together to encourage them and explain his intention, and spoke as follows:

“Peloponnesians, the character of the country we have come from, which has always owed its freedom to valor, and the fact that you are Dorians and the enemy you are about to fight are Ionians, whom you are accustomed to beat, need no further comment. But the plan of attack I propose to follow does deserve explanation, so that our venturing with a part of our forces instead of the whole may not damp your courage by the apparent disadvantage it puts you at. I imagine it is the poor opinion the enemy has of us, and his having no idea that anyone will come out to engage him, that has made him march up to the place and look carelessly about him as he is doing, without noticing us. But the most successful soldier will always be the man who most happily detects a blunder like this, and who, carefully weighing his own means, makes his attack not so much by open and regular approaches as by seizing the opportunity of the moment. Such stratagems do the greatest service to our friends by most completely deceiving our enemies, and they have the most brilliant name in war. Therefore, while their careless confidence lasts, and while they are still thinking, as in my judgment they now are, more of retreat than of holding their position, while their spirit is slack and not strung up with expectation, I will take the men under my command and, if possible, surprise them and fall with a run upon their center. And you, Clearidas, afterwards, when you see me already upon them and, as is likely, spreading terror among them, take the Amphipolitans and the rest of the allies, suddenly open the gates, dash out at them, and hasten to engage as quickly as you can. That is our best chance of throwing them into a panic, as a fresh assailant has always more terrors for an enemy than the one he is already fighting. Show yourself a brave man, as a Spartan should; and you, allies, follow him like men. Remember that zeal, honor, and obedience mark the good soldier, and that this day will make you either free men and allies of Lacedaemon, or slaves of Athens. Even if you escape without personal loss of liberty or life, your bondage will be on harsher terms than before, and you will also hinder the liberation of the rest of the Hellenes. Let there be no cowardice on your part, then, seeing the greatness of the issues at stake; and I will show that what I preach to others I can practice myself.”

After this brief speech Brasidas prepared for the sally himself, and placed the rest with Clearidas at the Thracian gates to support him, as had been agreed. Meanwhile he had been seen coming down from Cerdylium and then in the city, which is overlooked from outside, sacrificing near the temple of Athene. In short, all his movements had been observed, and word was brought to Cleon, who had at that moment gone on to look about him. The report was that the whole force of the enemy could be seen in the town, and that the feet of horses and of many men were visible under the gates, as if a sally were intended. On hearing this he went up to look, and when he had looked, he was unwilling to risk the decisive step of a battle before his reinforcements came up, and he fancied he would have time to retire. He ordered the retreat to be sounded and sent word to the men to carry it out by moving on the left wing in the direction of Eion, which was indeed the only way practicable. This was not quick enough for him, however, so he joined the retreat in person and made the right wing wheel around, thus turning its unarmed side to the enemy. It was then that Brasidas, seeing the Athenian force in motion and his opportunity come, said to the men with him and the rest: “Those fellows will never stand before us; one can see that by the way their spears and heads are going. Troops that behave as they do seldom stand a charge. Quick, someone, open the gates I spoke of, and let us be out and at them with no fear for the result.” Accordingly he issued out by the palisade gate and by the first gate in the long wall then existing, and ran at top speed along the straight road, where the trophy now stands as you go by the steepest part of the hill. He fell upon the center of the Athenians and routed it, for they were panic-stricken by their own disorder and astounded at his audacity. At the same moment Clearidas, carrying out his orders, issued out from the Thracian gates to support him, and also attacked the enemy. The result was that the Athenians, suddenly and unexpectedly attacked on both sides, fell into confusion. Their left, toward Eion, which had already got on some distance, at once broke and fled. It was in full retreat, and Brasidas was passing on to attack the right, when he received a wound. His fall was not perceived by the Athenians, since those near him took him up and carried him off the field. The Athenian right made a better stand. Cleon, who from the first had had no thought of fighting, fled at once and was overtaken and slain by a Myrcinian targeteer. But his infantry formed in close order on the hill and twice or thrice repulsed the attacks of Clearidas. They did not finally give way until they were surrounded and routed by the missiles of the Myrcinian and Chalcidian horse and the targeteers. Thus the whole Athenian army was now in flight. Those who escaped being killed in the battle, or by the Chalcidian horse and the targeteers, dispersed among the hills and made their way to Eion with difficulty. The men who had taken up and rescued Brasidas brought him into the town with the breath still in him. He lived to hear of the victory of his troops, and not long after he died. The rest of the army, returning with Clearidas from the pursuit, stripped the dead and set up a trophy.

After this all the allies attended in arms and buried Brasidas at public expense in the city, in front of what is now the marketplace. The Amphipolitans enclosed his tomb, and ever afterwards they sacrifice to him as a hero and have given him the honor of games and annual offerings. They made him the founder of their colony, and pulled down the Hagnonic erections and obliterated everything that could be taken as a memorial of Hagnon’s founding the place. For they considered that Brasidas had been their preserver. They were courting the alliance of Lacedaemon for fear of Athens, and in their present hostile relations with Athens they could no longer pay Hagnon his honors with the same advantage or satisfaction. They also gave the Athenians back their dead. About six hundred of the Athenians had fallen and only seven of the enemy, because there had been no regular engagement, only the affair of accident and panic that I have described. After taking up their dead, the Athenians sailed off home, while Clearidas and his troops remained to arrange matters at Amphipolis.

About the same time three Lacedaemonians — Ramphias, Autocharidas, and Epicydidas — led a reinforcement of nine hundred heavy infantry to the towns in the direction of Thrace. They arrived at Heraclea in Trachis and reformed matters there as seemed good to them. While they delayed there, this battle took place, and so the summer ended.

With the beginning of the winter following, Ramphias and his companions advanced as far as Pierium in Thessaly. But the Thessalians opposed their further advance, and Brasidas, whom they had come to reinforce, was dead. They therefore turned back home, thinking that the moment had gone by, since the Athenians were defeated and gone and they themselves were not equal to carrying out the designs of Brasidas. The main cause of their return, however, was that they knew that when they set out Lacedaemonian opinion was really in favor of peace.

Indeed it so happened that directly after the battle of Amphipolis and the retreat of Ramphias from Thessaly, both sides ceased to prosecute the war and turned their attention to peace. Athens had suffered severely at Delium, and again shortly afterwards at Amphipolis. She no longer had the confidence in her strength that had made her refuse to treat before, in the belief of ultimate victory inspired by her success at the moment. Besides, she was afraid that her allies, tempted by her reverses, would rebel more generally, and she repented of having let go the splendid opportunity for peace that the affair of Pylos had offered. Lacedaemon, on the other hand, found that the course of the war falsified her notion that a few years would suffice to overthrow the power of the Athenians by devastating their land. She had suffered on the island a disaster hitherto unknown at Sparta. She saw her country plundered from Pylos and Cythera. The Helots were deserting, and she was in constant apprehension that those who remained in Peloponnese would rely upon those outside and take advantage of the situation to renew their old attempts at revolution. Besides this, as chance would have it, her thirty years’ truce with the Argives was about to expire, and they refused to renew it unless Cynuria was restored to them; so it seemed impossible to fight Argos and Athens at once. She also suspected some of the cities in Peloponnese of intending to go over to the enemy, and that was indeed the case.

These considerations made both sides disposed to an accommodation. The Lacedaemonians were probably the more eager, since they ardently desired to recover the men taken on the island. The Spartans among these belonged to the first families and were therefore related to the governing body in Lacedaemon. Negotiations had been begun directly after the capture, but the Athenians, in their hour of triumph, would not consent to any reasonable terms. After their defeat at Delium, however, Lacedaemon knew that they would now be more inclined to listen, and at once concluded the armistice for a year, during which the two sides were to confer and see whether a longer period could be agreed upon.

Now, however, after the Athenian defeat at Amphipolis and the deaths of Cleon and Brasidas, who had been the two principal opponents of peace on either side — Brasidas because of the success and honor that war gave him, Cleon because he thought that if tranquillity were restored his crimes would be more open to detection and his slanders less credited — the foremost candidates for power in either city, Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, king of Lacedaemon, and Nicias, son of Niceratus, the most fortunate general of his time, each desired peace more ardently than ever. Nicias, while still happy and honored, wished to secure his good fortune. He wanted a present release from trouble for himself and his countrymen, and to hand down to posterity a name as an ever-successful statesman. He thought the way to do this was to keep out of danger and commit himself as little as possible to fortune, and that only peace made this keeping out of danger possible. Pleistoanax, for his part, was attacked by his enemies over his restoration, and they regularly held it up against him whenever any reverse befell his countrymen, as though his unjust restoration were the cause. The accusation was that he and his brother Aristocles had bribed the prophetess of Delphi to tell the Lacedaemonian deputations that arrived one after another at the temple to bring home the seed of the demigod son of Zeus from abroad, or else they would have to plow with a silver share. In this way, it was insisted, he had in time induced the Lacedaemonians to restore him, in the nineteenth year of his exile at Lycaeum, with the same dances and sacrifices with which they had instituted their kings upon the first settlement of Lacedaemon. He had gone to Lycaeum when banished on suspicion of having been bribed to retreat from Attica, and for fear of the Lacedaemonians he had built half his house within the consecrated precinct of Zeus. The smart of this accusation made him ardently desire a settlement. He reflected that in peace no disaster could occur, and that once Lacedaemon had recovered her men his enemies would have nothing to take hold of; whereas while war lasted, the highest station must always bear the scandal of everything that went wrong. Accordingly this winter was employed in conferences. As spring rapidly approached, the Lacedaemonians sent round orders to the cities to prepare for a fortified occupation of Attica, and held this as a sword over the heads of the Athenians to induce them to listen to their overtures. At last, after many claims had been urged on either side at the conferences, a peace was agreed on upon the following basis. Each party was to restore its conquests, but Athens was to keep Nisaea. Her demand for Plataea was met by the Thebans’ assertion that they had acquired the place not by force or treachery, but by the voluntary adhesion of its citizens upon agreement; and the same, according to the Athenian account, was the history of her acquisition of Nisaea. This arranged, the Lacedaemonians summoned their allies. All voted for peace except the Boeotians, Corinthians, Eleans, and Megarians, who did not approve of these proceedings. The Lacedaemonians nevertheless concluded the treaty and made peace, each of the contracting parties swearing to the following articles:
The Athenians and Lacedaemonians and their allies made a treaty, and swore to it, city by city, as follows:
1. Concerning the national temples, all who wish shall have free passage by land and by sea to sacrifice, travel, consult, and attend the oracle or games, according to the customs of their countries.

2. The temple and shrine of Apollo at Delphi, and the Delphians, shall be governed by their own laws, shall tax themselves through their own state, and shall be judged by their own judges, both land and people, according to the custom of their country.

3. The treaty shall be binding for fifty years upon the Athenians and the allies of the Athenians, and upon the Lacedaemonians and the allies of the Lacedaemonians, without fraud or harm by land or by sea.

4. It shall not be lawful for the Lacedaemonians and their allies to take up arms with intent to do harm against the Athenians and their allies, nor for the Athenians and their allies against the Lacedaemonians and their allies, in any way or by any means whatsoever. But if any difference arises between them, they are to have recourse to law and oaths, as the parties may agree.

5. The Lacedaemonians and their allies shall give back Amphipolis to the Athenians. In the case of cities given up by the Lacedaemonians to the Athenians, however, the inhabitants shall be allowed to go where they please and take their property with them. The cities shall be independent, paying only the tribute of Aristides. After the treaty has been concluded, the Athenians and their allies shall not be allowed to make war against them so long as the tribute is paid. The cities in question are Argilus, Stagirus, Acanthus, Scolus, Olynthus, and Spartolus. These cities shall be neutral, allies neither of the Lacedaemonians nor of the Athenians; but if the cities consent, the Athenians may make them their allies, provided always that the cities themselves wish it. The Mecybernaeans, Sanaeans, and Singaeans shall inhabit their own cities, as shall the Olynthians and Acanthians. The Lacedaemonians and their allies shall give back Panactum to the Athenians.

6. The Athenians shall give back Coryphasium, Cythera, Methana, and the Lacedaemonians who are in the prison at Athens or elsewhere in the Athenian dominions. They shall also let go the Peloponnesians besieged in Scione, all others in Scione who are allies of the Lacedaemonians, all whom Brasidas sent in there, and any others of the allies of the Lacedaemonians who may be in the prison at Athens or elsewhere in the Athenian dominions.
7. The Lacedaemonians and their allies shall in the same way give back any of the Athenians or their allies whom they may have in their hands.
8. In the case of Scione, Torone, and Sermylium, and any other cities that the Athenians hold, the Athenians may adopt such measures as they please.

9. The Athenians shall swear an oath to the Lacedaemonians and their allies, city by city. Every man shall swear by the most binding oath of his country, seventeen men from each city. The oath shall be this: “I will abide by this agreement and treaty honestly and without deceit.” The Lacedaemonians and their allies shall swear the same oath to the Athenians, and both parties shall renew the oath every year. Pillars shall be erected at Olympia, Pythia, the Isthmus, at Athens on the Acropolis, and at Lacedaemon in the temple at Amyclae.
10. If anything is forgotten, whatever it be, and on whatever point, it shall be consistent with their oath for both parties, the Athenians and Lacedaemonians, to alter it as they see fit.

The treaty begins from the ephoralty of Pleistolas at Lacedaemon, on the 27th day of the month of Artemisium, and from the archonship of Alcaeus at Athens, on the 25th day of the month of Elaphebolion. The men who took the oath and poured the libations for the Lacedaemonians were Pleistoanax, Agis, Pleistolas, Damagetis, Chionis, Metagenes, Acanthus, Daithus, Ischagoras, Philocharidas, Zeuxidas, Antippus, Tellis, Alcinadas, Empedias, Menas, and Laphilus; for the Athenians, Lampon, Isthmonicus, Nicias, Laches, Euthydemus, Procles, Pythodorus, Hagnon, Myrtilus, Thrasycles, Theagenes, Aristocrates, Iolcius, Timocrates, Leon, Lamachus, and Demosthenes.

This treaty was made in the spring, just at the end of winter, directly after the city festival of Dionysus, ten years to within a few days from the first invasion of Attica and the beginning of this war. This must be reckoned by the seasons rather than by trusting the list of the names of magistrates or holders of offices of honor that are used to mark past events. Accuracy is impossible where an event may have occurred at the beginning, or the middle, or any other point of their tenure of office. But if one computes by summers and winters, the method adopted in this history, each of them amounting to half a year, it will be found that this first war contained ten summers and as many winters.

The Lacedaemonians, whose lot it was to begin the work of restitution, immediately set free all the prisoners of war they held. They then sent Ischagoras, Menas, and Philocharidas as envoys to the towns in the direction of Thrace. Their orders were that Clearidas should hand Amphipolis over to the Athenians, and that the rest of the allies should each accept the treaty as it applied to them. The allies disliked its terms and refused. Clearidas, too, wanted to oblige the Chalcidians and would not hand over the town; he claimed he could not do so against their will. He hurried in person to Lacedaemon with envoys from the place, to defend his disobedience against any accusations that Ischagoras and his companions might make, and to find out whether it was too late for the agreement to be altered. He found the Lacedaemonians already bound, and quickly set out back with their instructions: to hand over the place if possible, or at all events to bring out the Peloponnesians who were in it.

The allies happened to be present in person at Lacedaemon, and the Lacedaemonians now asked those who had not accepted the treaty to adopt it. They refused for the same reasons as before, unless a fairer treaty than this one were agreed upon. Since they stood firm, the Lacedaemonians dismissed them and decided instead to form an alliance with the Athenians. They thought that Argos, which had refused the request of Ampelidas and Lichas to renew the treaty, would no longer be formidable without Athens. They thought also that the rest of Peloponnese would be most likely to keep quiet if the coveted alliance of Athens were closed to them. So, after conference with the Athenian ambassadors, an alliance was agreed upon and oaths were exchanged, on the following terms:
1. The Lacedaemonians shall be allies of the Athenians for fifty years.

2. Should any enemy invade the territory of Lacedaemon and injure the Lacedaemonians, the Athenians shall give help in the most effective way they can, according to their power. If the invader has gone after plundering the country, that city shall be an enemy of both Lacedaemon and Athens, shall be punished by both, and neither shall make peace without the other. All this shall be done honestly, loyally, and without fraud.

3. Should any enemy invade the territory of Athens and injure the Athenians, the Lacedaemonians shall give them help in the most effective way they can, according to their power. If the invader has gone after plundering the country, that city shall be an enemy of both Lacedaemon and Athens, shall be punished by both, and neither shall make peace without the other. All this shall be done honestly, loyally, and without fraud.
4. Should the slave population rise in revolt, the Athenians shall help the Lacedaemonians with all their might, according to their power.

5. The same persons shall swear this treaty on either side who swore to the other. It shall be renewed every year, the Lacedaemonians going to Athens for the Dionysia and the Athenians going to Lacedaemon for the Hyacinthia, and each party shall set up a pillar: at Lacedaemon near the statue of Apollo at Amyclae, and at Athens on the Acropolis near the statue of Athene. If the Lacedaemonians and Athenians decide to add anything to the alliance or remove anything from it, it shall be consistent with their oaths for both parties to do so, at their discretion.

The Lacedaemonians who took the oath were Pleistoanax, Agis, Pleistolas, Damagetus, Chionis, Metagenes, Acanthus, Daithus, Ischagoras, Philocharidas, Zeuxidas, Antippus, Alcinadas, Tellis, Empedias, Menas, and Laphilus; the Athenians were Lampon, Isthmionicus, Laches, Nicias, Euthydemus, Procles, Pythodorus, Hagnon, Myrtilus, Thrasycles, Theagenes, Aristocrates, Iolcius, Timocrates, Leon, Lamachus, and Demosthenes.

This alliance was made not long after the treaty. The Athenians gave the men from the island back to the Lacedaemonians, and the summer of the eleventh year began. With this the history of the first war is complete; it filled the whole of the ten years just described.
